title: The Italian Game
eyebrow: Opening study · one line, twelve moves
standfirst: Chess's oldest recorded opening, and still the clearest place to learn what the first ten moves are actually for. Step through it — every move is here because of an idea, not because a book said so.

steps.title: Thirty-two pieces, no decisions yet
body: Every opening is an argument about four squares: e4, d4, e5 and d5. Control them and your pieces radiate outward; concede them and you spend the game defending.
Watch what each move below is really doing. Almost none of them are about the piece that moves — they're about the squares it starts to cover.

steps.title: One move, two pieces freed
body: The pawn claims a centre square, but the real gain is behind it: the queen and the light-squared bishop both now have open diagonals. No other first move releases two pieces at once.
This is why 1.e4 has been the most played move in recorded chess for four centuries.

steps.title: Black refuses to give ground
body: The mirror answer. Black stakes an equal claim in the centre rather than conceding space and counterattacking later, which is what the Sicilian, French and Caro-Kann all do instead.
Symmetry isn't passive here — it's the most direct way to say I want the same things you want.

steps.title: Develop, and ask a question
body: The knight comes to its best square and attacks e5 on the way. The strongest developing moves do two jobs, because a move that only develops gives your opponent a free hand.
Knights before bishops, generally: a knight's best square is usually obvious this early, a bishop's often isn't.

steps.title: Defend with a piece you wanted to move anyway
body: The e5 pawn needed help, and this is the way to give it: the knight defends and develops toward the centre.
Compare 2…d6, which also defends but locks in the dark-squared bishop. The best defensive move is the one you'd have played regardless.

steps.title: The Italian bishop finds its diagonal
body: This is the move the opening is named for. The bishop's diagonal ends on f7 — the one square in Black's camp defended by nothing but the king.
It isn't an immediate threat. It's a standing one, and it shapes every tactic in this opening for the next twenty moves.

steps.title: The Giuoco Piano — “the quiet game”
body: Black copies the idea exactly, aiming at f2, White's matching soft spot. The position is now perfectly symmetrical and both sides are fully justified.
The name is four hundred years old and slightly misleading — it stays quiet only as long as both players want it to.

steps.title: A small move with a large plan
body: It develops nothing, and that's the point of showing it. c3 prepares d4: once the d-pawn advances, c3 is there to recapture and hold a broad pawn centre.
Openings aren't only about developing fastest. Sometimes a tempo buys a structure that pays for itself all game.

steps.title: Develop toward the enemy pawn
body: The last minor piece comes out, and it comes out hitting e4. Black is now one move from castling.
Notice the pattern on both sides: nobody has moved a piece twice, and nobody has brought the queen out. Six moves in, that's what a healthy position looks like.

steps.title: The modern choice: build, don't lunge
body: The sharp 5.d4 exists and leads to enormous complications. 5.d3 instead defends e4, frees the dark-squared bishop, and keeps the centre stable — the Giuoco Pianissimo, “the very quiet game”.
It's the top-level preference today for a reason: a position you understand beats a position you've memorised.

steps.title: Black shores up the centre
body: Propping up e5 and opening the c8 bishop's diagonal. The structures are now locked in and both sides know what they're playing for.
This is where memory ends and chess begins — from here you're navigating by plans, not by recall.

steps.title: Six moves, and everything is where it should be
body: Two pawns in the centre, three minor pieces out, the king safe, and the rook joining the game. That's the whole job of an opening — you've done it without memorising a single trap.

From here the standard plan is Re1, then the slow knight tour Nbd2–f1–g3, bringing the last piece to the kingside where the attack will be. Play this line twenty times and you'll start seeing it before you calculate it.
